The vertex is the screened potential change of a phonon, the coupling that density-functional perturbation theory (DFPT) computes, and the phonons are nuclei that interact through the electron-screened Coulomb interaction.

What you need: the phonons of Section A.1, in particular the displacement operator ; from Section A.2, the Bloch states, the electron operators (with its background box on second quantization), the matrix element $g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)$, and the jellium model of a metal with its Thomas–Fermi screening; the screened vertex and the electronic dielectric function of DFPT in Section A.3; and the Born charges, dielectric constants and Fröhlich coupling of Section A.4. You should be at ease with the Heisenberg picture of quantum mechanics. Background boxes teach the electron propagator and its poles, Dyson equations, and Hedin's equations with the GW approximation. The functional derivatives that the theory uses are defined in the main text, and a derivation box shows how they produce the self-energy.1

The picture: two screening clouds

The electron–phonon calculations of Sections A.2–A.4 rest on three simplifications. The coupling $g$ is computed from the Kohn–Sham potential, so it inherits the approximate exchange–correlation functional. The phonons are computed in the Born–Oppenheimer approximation of Section A.1, which assumes that the electrons follow the nuclei instantly; this is doubtful when an electronic excitation costs as little as a phonon, as in metals and doped semiconductors. And the electrons screen the potential of a moving nucleus as if the nucleus were frozen. Beyond these, electrons and phonons change each other: the phonons shift and broaden the electron energies, and the electrons shift and broaden the phonon frequencies. An exact theory must therefore determine both together, self-consistently.

The review answers with a many-body theory of electrons and nuclei, built with Schwinger's functional-derivative method (explained below), in the form given by Baym (1961) and by Hedin and Lundqvist (1969). Its central object is the screened Coulomb interaction, and its central result is that this interaction contains the motion of the lattice.

Physical picture: two screening clouds

Place a test charge inside a polar crystal such as GaAs. Within about a femtosecond the electrons rearrange around it and reduce its field by a factor $\varepsilon_\infty$$\,=10.9$, the electronic dielectric constant. The interaction reduced in this way is the screened interaction of a GW calculation. If the charge stays in place for longer than a period of the optical phonons, about 0.1 ps, the ions shift as well, and the field drops further, to $1/\varepsilon_{\mathrm s}$ of its bare value, with the static dielectric constant $\varepsilon_{\mathrm s}=12.9$. A charge that moves or varies in time therefore carries a fast electronic cloud and a slow ionic one. The theory of this section puts both clouds into one screened interaction and treats the slow ionic cloud as a propagating quantum object: the phonon.

The plan of the section:

  1. write the Hamiltonian of electrons and nuclei, coupled by one instantaneous Coulomb interaction;
  2. see in three simple models what moving ions do to the interaction between electrons;
  3. define the electron propagator and its self-energy, and derive the equation for the screened interaction;
  4. split the screened interaction into an electronic part and a lattice part, and write the lattice part with phonons;
  5. derive the equation of motion of the phonons;
  6. collect everything into the closed set of Hedin–Baym equations.

One Hamiltonian, one instantaneous interaction

The electrons are identical fermions. They are described by a field operator $\hat\psi(\br)$, which removes an electron at the point $\br$, and its conjugate $\hat\psi^\dagger(\br)$, which adds one. In terms of the Bloch states $\psi_{n\bk}$ and the operators $c_{n\bk}$ of Section A.2, $\hat\psi(\br)=\sum_{n\bk}\psi_{n\bk}(\br)\,c_{n\bk}$. The electron density operator is $\hat n^{\rme}(\br)=\hat\psi^\dagger(\br)\hat\psi(\br)$. Spin is suppressed. The field operators carry a spin label that is not written, and the density operator contains the sum over both spin directions. Nothing in this section depends on spin, so a quantity such as the propagator below is the same for both directions, and a factor 2 is written where the spin sum is carried out.

The nuclei are treated differently. In a solid each nucleus stays near its own site, so the nuclei can be told apart and labelled by cell and basis atom, $\ell\kappa$, exactly as in Section A.1. Their equilibrium positions $\btau_{\ell\kappa}$ are external parameters, taken from experiment or from a structural relaxation, a calculation that moves the atoms until every force vanishes. The dynamical variables are the displacement operators $\hat\bu_{\ell\kappa}$ and their conjugate momenta $\hat\bP_{\ell\kappa}$ (not the dipoles $\mathbf p_{\ell\kappa}$ of Section A.4). Phonons, the quanta of the displacements, appear later. The charge of nucleus $\kappa$ is $Z_\kappa e$, with $Z_\kappa$ as in Section A.2: the atomic number, or the ionic valence when the core electrons are frozen into a pseudopotential.

It is convenient to count all charges in units of the electron's charge $-e$: an electron counts $+1$, a nucleus $-Z_\kappa$. The density of charge in these units is

$$\begin{aligned}\hat n&=\hat n^{\rme}+\hat n^{\ion},\\ \hat n^{\ion}&=-\sum_{\ell\kappa}Z_\kappa\,\delta(\br-\btau_{\ell\kappa}-\hat\bu_{\ell\kappa}),\end{aligned} \tag{A5.1}$$

and the charge density itself is $-e\hat n$. The nuclear part $\hat n^{\ion}$ is negative and depends on the displacements: its delta functions sit at the instantaneous positions of the nuclei. With this bookkeeping, $\int\dd^3r'\,v(\br-\br')\,\langle\hat n(\br')\rangle$ is the potential energy of an electron at $\br$ in the field of all charges, where $v(\br)=e^2/|\br|$ is the bare Coulomb interaction of Section A.3.

The Hamiltonian is the kinetic energy of the electrons and of the nuclei plus the Coulomb energy of every pair of charges:2

$$\begin{aligned}\hat H={}&\hat T^{\rme}+\hat T^{\ion}\\&+\frac12\int\dd^3r\,\dd^3r'\,v(\br-\br')\\&\quad\times\hat n^{\rme}(\br)\big[\hat n^{\rme}(\br')-\delta(\br-\br')\big]\\&+\int\dd^3r\,\hat n^{\rme}(\br)\,\hat V^{\mathrm{en}}(\br)\\&+\frac12\sum_{\ell\kappa\neq\ell'\kappa'}Z_\kappa Z_{\kappa'}\,v\big(\btau_{\ell\kappa}+\hat\bu_{\ell\kappa}\\&\qquad-\btau_{\ell'\kappa'}-\hat\bu_{\ell'\kappa'}\big).\end{aligned} \tag{A5.2}$$
$\hat T^{\rme}$
kinetic energy of the electrons, $-(\hbar^2/2m_{\mathrm e})\int\dd^3r\,\hat\psi^\dagger\nabla^2\hat\psi$, with $m_{\mathrm e}$ the electron mass
$\hat T^{\ion}$
kinetic energy of the nuclei, $\sum_{\ell\kappa}\hat\bP_{\ell\kappa}^2/2M_\kappa$, with $M_\kappa$ the mass of nucleus $\kappa$
$\hat V^{\mathrm{en}}(\br)$
potential energy of an electron in the field of all nuclei, $\int\dd^3r'\,v(\br-\br')\,\hat n^{\ion}(\br')$ $=-\sum_{\ell\kappa}Z_\kappa e^2/|\br-\btau_{\ell\kappa}-\hat\bu_{\ell\kappa}|$: the $V^{\mathrm{en}}$ of Section A.2 with the nuclei at their instantaneous positions, hence an operator (eV)

The last three terms of are one interaction, $v$, acting between electrons, between electrons and nuclei, and between nuclei. The term $-\delta(\br-\br')$ removes the interaction of each electron with itself, and the nuclei, which are distinguishable, are counted pair by pair. Together the three terms are $\frac12\int\dd^3r\,\dd^3r'\,v(\br-\br')\,\hat n(\br)\hat n(\br')$ with all self-interactions removed. Nothing else couples the particles: there is no vector potential, no magnetic force and no photon.

The formulas below involve functions of two or more points in space and time. A number stands for a point and its time, $1\equiv(\br_1,t_1)$; an integral $\int\dd1$ runs over $\dd^3r_1\,\dd t_1$, and $\int\dd(34)$ is short for $\int\dd3\,\dd4$; and $1^+\equiv(\br_1,t_1+\eta)$ is the point $1$ an instant later, with $\eta\to0^+$. In this notation the Coulomb interaction is

$$v(12)=v(\br_1-\br_2)\,\delta(t_1-t_2). \tag{A5.3}$$

The delta function in time says that the interaction is instantaneous: a charge moved at time $t_1$ is felt everywhere at that same time. Every bare interaction in this section is this one. Part A therefore describes only the electrostatic field of the charges, which is longitudinal: in Fourier space it points along the wavevector $\bq$, as the atoms move along $\bq$ in a longitudinal mode. The screened interactions built from it below are not instantaneous, because the screening clouds take time to form.

Moving ions in three simple models

Before the general theory, three models show what the motion of the nuclei does to the interaction between electrons. They share three quantities. The screened interaction $W$ is the potential energy that an electron feels because of a unit charge of the electron's sign at another point, including the response of all other charges. $W^{\rme}$ is the same quantity when only the electrons respond and the nuclei stay at their sites. Their difference, $W^{\ph}=W-W^{\rme}$, is what the moving nuclei add. The precise definitions follow in the subsections on screening.3

Two electrons and a row of ions

Take a row of ions of charge $Ze$ and mass $M$, a distance $a$ apart. Each ion is held near its site by a spring of frequency $\omega_0$ and moves independently of the others: a set of Einstein oscillators, the simplest model of an optical branch without dispersion (its frequency does not depend on the wavevector). Two electrons move along a line parallel to the row. Electrons and ions interact through the electron-screened interaction $W^{\rme}$, here in the screened Coulomb form $W^{\rme}(r)=(e^2/r)\,\ee^{-k_{\mathrm{TF}}r}$ of Section A.2: the other electrons cut the interaction off beyond a screening length $1/k_{\mathrm{TF}}$, where $k_{\mathrm{TF}}$ is the Thomas–Fermi wavevector (1.3 Å⁻¹ in potassium, 2.1 Å⁻¹ in aluminium).

Electron 1 at $x_1$ attracts ion $\ell$ with a force $\bF_\ell(x_1)$. Let the charge at $x_1$ oscillate in time as $\cos\omega t$; any time dependence, such as an electron passing by, is a superposition of such components. Ion $\ell$ then moves like a driven oscillator, with displacement $\bF_\ell(x_1)/\big[M(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)\big]$: in phase with the force below resonance and against it above.

When ion $\ell$ moves by $\bu_\ell$, the interaction energy of electron 2 with that ion changes by $-\bF_\ell(x_2)\cdot\bu_\ell$, because the force on the ion is minus the gradient of their interaction energy with respect to the ion's position. Summing over the ions gives the extra potential energy of electron 2 per unit charge of electron 1:

$$\begin{aligned}&W^{\ph}(x_2,x_1;\omega)\\&\quad=\sum_\ell\frac{\bF_\ell(x_2)\cdot\bF_\ell(x_1)}{M\,(\omega^2-\omega_0^2)} .\end{aligned} \tag{A5.4}$$
$x_1$, $x_2$
positions of the two electrons along the row (Å)
$\bF_\ell(x)$
force on ion $\ell$ exerted by an electron at $x$, through the screened interaction (eV/Å)
$\omega_0$
frequency of each ion's spring; $\omega$ is the frequency at which the charge at $x_1$ oscillates (both in s⁻¹, quoted as $\hbar\omega$ in meV)

The formula has three factors: the force of electron 1 on an ion, the displacement of the ion per unit force at frequency $\omega$, and the change of the energy of electron 2 per unit displacement of the ion. This anatomy, a coupling at each end and an oscillator in between, is the anatomy of the general result .

The sign follows from the driven oscillator. When electron 2 is close to electron 1, the two forces on a nearby ion point the same way and the numerator is positive. Below resonance, $\omega<\omega_0$, the ions move toward electron 1 and gather positive charge near it, so $W^{\ph}<0$: the moving ions add an attraction between the electrons. Above resonance the ions move against the force and $W^{\ph}>0$. For $\omega\gg\omega_0$ the ions cannot follow and $W^{\ph}\to0$.

Whether the total $W=W^{\rme}+W^{\ph}$ is attractive depends on the size of $W^{\ph}$ against the screened repulsion. With the parameters of (sodium mass, $\hbar\omega_0=15$ meV, $k_{\mathrm{TF}}=1$ Å⁻¹, illustrative), the ions reduce the static repulsion at 2 Å from 0.97 to 0.54 eV, and at $\omega=0.8\,\omega_0$ they reverse it, to $-0.24$ eV.

A polar insulator

At long wavelengths a crystal acts as a homogeneous medium. A test charge whose density varies as $\ee^{\ii(\bq\cdot\br-\omega t)}$ then creates a potential reduced by the dielectric function $\varepsilon(\bq,\omega)$ of all charges, electrons and ions, so that $W(\bq,\omega)=v(q)/\varepsilon(\bq,\omega)$, with $v(q)=4\pi e^2/q^2$ the Fourier transform of the bare Coulomb interaction. The electrons contribute their own dielectric function, $\varepsilon^{\rme}$ of Section A.3; the ions add a term, found in three steps for a cubic crystal with two atoms per cell:

  1. In an optical mode at $\bq\to0$ the two sublattices move against each other, with relative displacement $\bu=\bu_1-\bu_2$. Each cell then carries the dipole $eZ^*\bu$, with $Z^*$ the Born effective charge of Section A.4, and responds to the macroscopic electric field $\bE$ as one oscillator of reduced mass $M_{\mathrm r}$: $M_{\mathrm r}\big(\ddot\bu+\omega_0^2\bu\big)=eZ^*\bE$.

    The frequency $\omega_0$ is that of the short-range restoring force alone, without the macroscopic field: the transverse optical frequency $\omega_{\mathrm{TO}}$, since a transverse mode creates no macroscopic field (Section A.4). The Born charge already includes the electrons that follow the ions, so the force on the cell is the Born charge times the macroscopic field.

  2. For a field that oscillates at $\omega$, $\bu=eZ^*\bE/\big[M_{\mathrm r}(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)\big]$, and the ionic polarization is $\bP^{\ion}=eZ^*\bu/\OV$.

    The polarization is the dipole per unit volume, one dipole per cell of volume $\OV$.

  3. The dielectric function is defined by $\varepsilon\,\bE=\varepsilon^{\rme}\bE+4\pi\bP^{\ion}$, which gives

    $$\begin{gathered}\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{\rme}+\frac{(\omega_{\mathrm p}^{\ion})^2}{\omega_0^2-\omega^2},\\ (\omega_{\mathrm p}^{\ion})^2=\frac{4\pi e^2Z^{*2}}{M_{\mathrm r}\OV}.\end{gathered} \tag{A5.5}$$
    The electrons' polarization is contained in $\varepsilon^{\rme}$; the ions add $4\pi\bP^{\ion}$ (Gaussian units).

$\omega_{\mathrm p}^{\ion}$ is the ionic plasma frequency: the frequency at which the ionic charge would oscillate if only the Coulomb force acted on it. For free ions of charge $Ze$ and mass $M$, one per volume $\OV$, it is $(\omega_{\mathrm p}^{\ion})^2=4\pi Z^2e^2/(M\OV)$; jellium below uses this form.4 For the polar crystal, $\omega_0=\omega_{\mathrm{TO}}$, and the electrons, whose gap lies far above the phonon energies, screen statically: $\varepsilon^{\rme}=$ $\varepsilon_\infty$. Then can be written as

$$\begin{aligned}\varepsilon(\omega)&=\varepsilon_\infty\,\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}^2-\omega^2}{\omega_{\mathrm{TO}}^2-\omega^2},\\ \omega_{\mathrm{LO}}^2&=\omega_{\mathrm{TO}}^2+\frac{(\omega_{\mathrm p}^{\ion})^2}{\varepsilon_\infty},\\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm s}&=\varepsilon(0)=\varepsilon_\infty\,\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}^2}{\omega_{\mathrm{TO}}^2}.\end{aligned} \tag{A5.6}$$

The second relation is the LO–TO splitting of Section A.4, , and the third is the Lyddane–Sachs–Teller relation between the static dielectric constant $\varepsilon_{\mathrm s}$ and the two frequencies $\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}$, $\omega_{\mathrm{TO}}$. With $W^{\rme}=v/\varepsilon_\infty$ and $W=v/\varepsilon(\omega)$, the lattice part follows in one line: $1/\varepsilon-1/\varepsilon_\infty=(\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}^2-\omega_{\mathrm{TO}}^2)/[\varepsilon_\infty(\omega^2-\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}^2)]$, and by the Lyddane–Sachs–Teller relation $(\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}^2-\omega_{\mathrm{TO}}^2)/\varepsilon_\infty=(1/\varepsilon_\infty-1/\varepsilon_{\mathrm s})\,\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}^2$. So

$$\begin{aligned}&W^{\rme}=\frac{v(q)}{\varepsilon_\infty},\qquad W=\frac{v(q)}{\varepsilon(\omega)},\\&W^{\ph}=v(q)\Big(\frac1{\varepsilon_\infty}-\frac1{\varepsilon_{\mathrm s}}\Big)\\&\qquad\quad\times\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}^2}{\omega^2-\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}^2}.\end{aligned} \tag{A5.7}$$

Four features matter.

  • A pole at LO, a zero at TO. $W$ is the interaction between charges, which acts through the longitudinal field, so it resonates with the longitudinal mode: its pole is at $\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}$, where $\varepsilon=0$, and it vanishes at $\omega_{\mathrm{TO}}$, where $\varepsilon$ diverges.
  • The lattice screens statically. At $\omega=0$, $W=v/\varepsilon_{\mathrm s}$ is smaller than $W^{\rme}=v/\varepsilon_\infty$, by 15 % in GaAs ($\varepsilon_{\mathrm s}=12.9$) and by 70 % in MgO ($\varepsilon_\infty=2.96$, $\varepsilon_{\mathrm s}=9.7$).
  • Attraction below LO. For $\omega<\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}$, $W^{\ph}<0$, as in the row of ions: the ionic cloud reduces the repulsion. Between TO and LO, in the Reststrahlen band (German for "residual rays": the crystal reflects infrared light in this band strongly), even the total $W$ is negative.
  • Two spectra. The energy lost by a fast charge, $-\mathrm{Im}\,(1/\varepsilon)$, peaks at $\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}$, while the infrared absorption, $\mathrm{Im}\,\varepsilon$, peaks at $\omega_{\mathrm{TO}}$.

Near its pole, $W^{\ph}$ of behaves as a constant divided by $\omega-\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}$, because $\omega^2-\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}^2\simeq2\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}(\omega-\omega_{\mathrm{LO}})$ there. That constant, the residue of the pole, is $v(q)(1/\varepsilon_\infty-1/\varepsilon_{\mathrm s})\,\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}/2$. It equals $\OV/\hbar$ times the square of Fröhlich's matrix element of Section A.4: a later subsection shows that $W^{\ph}$ is an LO phonon passed between two electrons, each coupled to it by Fröhlich's matrix element.5

Jellium with mobile ions

A simple metal such as sodium can be modelled as the jellium of Section A.2: an electron gas of uniform density $n^{\rme}_0$ in a uniform positive background. The density $n^{\rme}_0$ is the $n_0$ of Section A.2; the superscript separates it from the nuclear density. Here the background consists of ions that can move, with $Z$ electrons per ion and one ion per volume $\OV=Z/n^{\rme}_0$. Two frequencies set the scales. The electron gas displaced against the ions oscillates at the electronic plasma frequency $\omega_{\mathrm p}$; the ions displaced against the electrons, with nothing else to hold them, would oscillate at the ionic plasma frequency:

$$\begin{gathered}\omega_{\mathrm p}^2=\frac{4\pi n^{\rme}_0e^2}{m_{\mathrm e}},\\ (\omega_{\mathrm p}^{\ion})^2=\frac{4\pi Z^2e^2}{M\OV}.\end{gathered} \tag{A5.8}$$

In sodium ($Z=1$, $M=22.99$ amu, $\OV=37.7$ Å³), $\hbar\omega_{\mathrm p}=6.05$ eV and $\hbar\omega_{\mathrm p}^{\ion}=29.6$ meV. Since $n^{\rme}_0=Z/\OV$, their ratio is $(Zm_{\mathrm e}/M)^{1/2}=0.005$: the mass ratio separates the electronic and ionic time scales.

At phonon frequencies the electrons cross a wavelength faster than one period, $\omega\ll v_{\mathrm F}q$, with $v_{\mathrm F}$ the Fermi velocity, so they screen statically. The Thomas–Fermi screening of Section A.2 gives $\varepsilon^{\rme}(q)=1+k_{\mathrm{TF}}^2/q^2$, with $k_{\mathrm{TF}}^2=6\pi n^{\rme}_0e^2/E_{\mathrm F}=4k_{\mathrm F}/(\pi a_0)$ in terms of the Fermi energy $E_{\mathrm F}$, the Fermi wavevector $k_{\mathrm F}$ and the Bohr radius $a_0$$\,=0.529$ Å ($k_{\mathrm{TF}}=1.49$ Å⁻¹ in sodium). The ions are free, $\omega_0=0$ in :

$$\varepsilon(q,\omega)=1+\frac{k_{\mathrm{TF}}^2}{q^2}-\frac{(\omega_{\mathrm p}^{\ion})^2}{\omega^2}. \tag{A5.9}$$

Writing $\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{\rme}(q)\big[1-\omega_{\mathrm{LA}}^2(q)/\omega^2\big]$ and subtracting $W^{\rme}=v/\varepsilon^{\rme}$ gives

$$\begin{aligned}W&=\frac{v(q)}{\varepsilon^{\rme}(q)}\,\frac{\omega^2}{\omega^2-\omega_{\mathrm{LA}}^2(q)},\\ W^{\ph}&=\frac{v(q)}{\varepsilon^{\rme}(q)}\,\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{LA}}^2(q)}{\omega^2-\omega_{\mathrm{LA}}^2(q)},\\ \omega_{\mathrm{LA}}^2(q)&=\frac{(\omega_{\mathrm p}^{\ion})^2}{\varepsilon^{\rme}(q)}.\end{aligned} \tag{A5.10}$$

The pole $\omega_{\mathrm{LA}}(q)$ is the frequency of the one branch of jellium, a longitudinal one; transverse waves of a uniform charge meet no restoring force. Electronic screening turns the ionic plasma oscillation into sound. At small $q$, $\varepsilon^{\rme}\simeq k_{\mathrm{TF}}^2/q^2$ and

$$\begin{aligned}\omega_{\mathrm{LA}}(q)&\simeq v_{\mathrm s}q,\\ v_{\mathrm s}&=\frac{\omega_{\mathrm p}^{\ion}}{k_{\mathrm{TF}}}=v_{\mathrm F}\Big(\frac{Zm_{\mathrm e}}{3M}\Big)^{1/2},\end{aligned} \tag{A5.11}$$

the Bohm–Staver sound velocity $v_{\mathrm s}$. It is 3.0 km/s for sodium, close to the measured 3.2 km/s quoted in Section A.2, and 9.1 km/s for aluminium, against a measured 6.4 km/s: jellium ignores the lattice and the ion cores. The second form follows from $k_{\mathrm{TF}}^2=6\pi n^{\rme}_0e^2/E_{\mathrm F}$ and $E_{\mathrm F}=m_{\mathrm e}v_{\mathrm F}^2/2$.

Below $\omega_{\mathrm{LA}}(q)$ the total interaction is negative: two electrons that exchange less energy than a phonon attract each other, because the slow ionic cloud more than cancels their repulsion. For $\omega\to0$, $W\to0$: free ions screen a static charge completely. This frequency-dependent attraction is the effective interaction of Bardeen and Pines (1955), and it is the pairing interaction of superconductors (Section A.9). With Lindhard's dielectric function of Section A.2 in place of Thomas–Fermi, the dispersion acquires a kink at $q=2k_{\mathrm F}$, the Kohn anomaly (Section A.6).6

In all three models $W=W^{\rme}+W^{\ph}$, and $W^{\ph}$ has one anatomy: a squared coupling times the response of an oscillator, which has a pole (diverges) at a frequency of the ions. For the Einstein ions it is their spring frequency $\omega_0$; in the two media, where the ions interact through their own field, it is the frequency of their longitudinal motion, $\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}$ or $\omega_{\mathrm{LA}}(q)$. The rest of the section shows that this structure is exact.

The electron propagator and its self-energy

The theory is built around the time-ordered electron propagator, or Green's function, in the exact ground state $|0\rangle$ of the coupled electrons and nuclei, at zero temperature:

$$G(12)=-\frac{\ii}{\hbar}\,\langle\mathcal T\,\hat\psi(1)\,\hat\psi^\dagger(2)\rangle . \tag{A5.12}$$
$\langle\cdots\rangle$
expectation value in the ground state $|0\rangle$
$\hat\psi(1)$
the field operator in the Heisenberg picture, $\ee^{\ii\hat H\,t_1/\hbar}\hat\psi(\br_1)\,\ee^{-\ii\hat H\,t_1/\hbar}$
$\mathcal T$
time ordering: puts the later operator to the left, with a minus sign when two fermion operators are exchanged
$G(12)$
units 1/(energy × time × volume); in the Bloch basis and in frequency, 1/energy

For $t_1>t_2$, $\ii\hbar G(12)$ is the amplitude for an electron added at $\br_2$ to be found at $\br_1$ a time $t_1-t_2$ later; for $t_1<t_2$ it describes a hole, a missing electron, created at $\br_1$ and found at $\br_2$ a time $t_2-t_1$ later. Its poles in frequency are the energies needed to add or remove an electron: the band energies, shifted and broadened by the interactions. Every shift and broadening of a band energy by the electron–phonon coupling in Sections A.7 and A.8 (a renormalization) is read off $G$.

The electron propagator and its poles skip if familiar

For independent electrons in Bloch states the propagator is diagonal in $n\bk$. An empty state ($E_{n\bk}>\mu$) can only gain an electron, so $G^0_{n\bk}(t)=-(\ii/\hbar)\,\ee^{-\ii E_{n\bk}t/\hbar}$ for $t>0$ and zero before. An occupied state ($E_{n\bk}<\mu$) can only lose one, so its propagator is nonzero for $t<0$: a hole propagates backward in time. In frequency both cases read

$$G^0_{n\bk}(\omega)=\frac{1}{\hbar\omega-E_{n\bk}+\ii\eta\,\mathrm{sgn}(E_{n\bk}-\mu)} ,$$

where the sign of the infinitesimal $\eta$ comes from the time ordering: the pole of an empty state lies just below the real axis, that of an occupied state just above. Either way the pole sits at the band energy $E_{n\bk}$; the chemical potential $\mu$ only decides on which side of the real axis it lies.

Interactions change two things. The poles move, because adding an electron now also rearranges the others; and they leave the real axis, because the added electron can decay into other excitations. An excitation that lives for a time $\tau$ has its pole at $\hbar\omega=E-\ii\hbar/2\tau$, since its amplitude decays as $\ee^{-t/2\tau}$ and its probability as $\ee^{-t/\tau}$. Poles close to the real axis are the quasiparticles of Section A.2; the rest of the weight of $G$ forms a broad background and side peaks called satellites (Section A.7).

The retarded propagator describes the causal response to a perturbation: it vanishes for $t_1<t_2$, and all its poles lie below the real axis, $\hbar\omega\to\hbar\omega+\ii\eta$ for every state. At zero temperature the time-ordered and retarded functions share their real parts and differ only in the sign of the imaginary part below $\mu$, so a formula derived for one converts into the other. Many-body perturbation theory uses the time-ordered function because it is the one with simple diagram rules (the box on Dyson equations below).

$G$ follows from a simpler propagator through a Dyson equation:7

$$\begin{aligned}&G=G^0+G^0\Sigma G,\\&G(12)=G^0(12)\\&\;+\int\dd(34)\,G^0(13)\Sigma(34)G(42).\end{aligned} \tag{A5.13}$$
$G^0$
propagator of one electron moving in the static total potential $V^{\mathrm{tot}}$ of below, the Hartree potential of all charges
$\Sigma(12)$
the electron self-energy: everything beyond that potential, namely exchange, correlation and the coupling to the moving nuclei

In the Bloch basis, with $\Sigma$ diagonal, reads $G_{n\bk}(\omega)=1/[\hbar\omega-E^0_{n\bk}-\Sigma_{n\bk}(\omega)]$, where $E^0_{n\bk}$ is a band energy of the reference propagator: the real part of $\Sigma_{n\bk}$ shifts the pole and the imaginary part gives its lifetime. In practice the reference is often the Kohn–Sham band structure of Section A.2, whose potential already contains the exchange–correlation potential $V^{\mathrm{xc}}$; $\Sigma$ is then replaced by $\Sigma-V^{\mathrm{xc}}$.

Dyson equations skip if familiar

Let an electron propagate freely, and let some process scatter it from point 4 to point 3 with amplitude $\Sigma(34)$. The full propagator from 2 to 1 is the free one, plus free propagation from 2 to 4, one scattering and free propagation from 3 to 1, plus two scatterings, and so on:

$$\begin{aligned}G&=G^0+G^0\Sigma G^0+G^0\Sigma G^0\Sigma G^0+\dots\\&=G^0+G^0\Sigma\big(G^0+G^0\Sigma G^0+\dots\big)\\&=G^0+G^0\Sigma G,\end{aligned}$$

where every product is an integral over the internal points, as written out in . The series is geometric, and in the Bloch basis, with $\Sigma$ diagonal, it sums to $1/(\hbar\omega-E^0_{n\bk}-\Sigma_{n\bk})$, since $G^0_{n\bk}=1/(\hbar\omega-E^0_{n\bk})$. The self-energy must contain only processes that cannot be cut in two by cutting a single $G^0$: such processes are irreducible. A reducible piece is already a repetition of irreducible ones and would be counted twice.

The same structure returns for every propagator in this primer: the screened interaction $W$, built from the bare $v$ and the polarizability, below; the phonon propagator in Section A.6; the photon propagator in Part B. In Feynman diagrams a propagator is a line, a self-energy is a blob, a product is a chain, and the internal points are integrated over.

A probe that acts on every charge

To find $\Sigma$, the review follows Schwinger. Add a weak external potential energy $V^{\mathrm{ext}}(\br,t)$ that acts on every charge, through the term $\int\dd^3r\,\hat n(\br)\,V^{\mathrm{ext}}(\br,t)$ in the Hamiltonian; follow how everything responds to it; and set it to zero at the end. Since $\hat n$ counts charge in units of $-e$, the probe gives an electron the energy $V^{\mathrm{ext}}$ and nucleus $\kappa$ the energy $-Z_\kappa V^{\mathrm{ext}}$. Because $\hat n$ contains electrons and nuclei, two quantities include the nuclei from the start. The first is the total potential, the potential energy of an electron in the mean field of all charges (the field of their average density $\langle\hat n\rangle$) plus the probe:

$$\begin{aligned}V^{\mathrm{tot}}(1)={}&V^{\mathrm{ext}}(1)\\&+\int\dd2\,v(12)\,\langle\hat n(2)\rangle .\end{aligned} \tag{A5.14}$$

The second is the inverse dielectric function, which says how much of a change of the probe survives in the total potential:8

$$\varepsilon^{-1}(12)=\frac{\delta V^{\mathrm{tot}}(1)}{\delta V^{\mathrm{ext}}(2)} . \tag{A5.15}$$

Here $\delta/\delta V^{\mathrm{ext}}(2)$ is a functional derivative. A small change $\delta V^{\mathrm{ext}}$ of the probe changes the total potential by $\delta V^{\mathrm{tot}}(1)=\int\dd2\,\varepsilon^{-1}(12)\,\delta V^{\mathrm{ext}}(2)$, so $\varepsilon^{-1}(12)$ is the change of $V^{\mathrm{tot}}$ at 1 per unit change of the probe at the single space-time point 2. Since the nuclei respond to the probe as well, $\varepsilon^{-1}$ contains the screening by the lattice together with the screening by the electrons.

One identity makes the probe useful. A change of the probe at point 3 enters the time evolution through the probe term of the Hamiltonian, whose integrand at point 3 is $\hat n(3)V^{\mathrm{ext}}(3)$. By first-order time-dependent perturbation theory it therefore changes every time-ordered expectation value by inserting the density fluctuation $\delta\hat n(3)=\hat n(3)-\langle\hat n(3)\rangle$:

$$\begin{aligned}&\frac{\delta\langle\mathcal T\hat A(1)\hat B(2)\rangle}{\delta V^{\mathrm{ext}}(3)}\\&\quad=-\frac{\ii}{\hbar}\,\langle\mathcal T\,\delta\hat n(3)\,\hat A(1)\hat B(2)\rangle\end{aligned}$$

for any operators $\hat A$ and $\hat B$, one of which may be absent. This is Schwinger's identity. The mean value is subtracted because the probe also changes the normalization of the state. The identity turns every response to the probe into a correlation function of the density.

The third quantity is the vertex function,

$$\Lambda(123)=-\frac{\delta G^{-1}(12)}{\delta V^{\mathrm{tot}}(3)} , \tag{A5.16}$$

where $G^{-1}$ is the inverse of $G$ as an integral kernel, $\int\dd2\,G(12)\,G^{-1}(23)=\delta(13)$, with $\delta(13)=\delta(\br_1-\br_3)\,\delta(t_1-t_3)$. The vertex says how the propagator responds to a change of the total potential at point 3. For an electron that responds only to the potential at its own position it would be $\Lambda(123)=\delta(12)\delta(13)$; the corrections describe how the change of the potential also rearranges the other electrons. With these definitions the equation of motion of $G$ takes the Dyson form , with

$$\begin{aligned}&\Sigma(12)=\ii\hbar\int\dd(34)\,G(13)\\&\qquad\times\Lambda(324)\,W(41^+),\\&W(12)=\int\dd3\,\varepsilon^{-1}(13)\,v(32).\end{aligned} \tag{A5.17}$$
$W(12)$
the screened interaction: the bare $v$ screened by all charges, electrons and nuclei; it is symmetric, $W(12)=W(21)$. $W(\br_1,\br_2;\omega)$ is an energy (eV), like $v(\br)$

The self-energy describes an electron that propagates while it interacts with itself through the screened interaction, with the vertex at one end. The factor $\ii\hbar$ appears because $G$ carries $1/\hbar$. The vertex obeys its own equation:

$$\begin{aligned}&\Lambda(123)=\delta(12)\delta(13)\\&\quad+\int\dd(4567)\,\frac{\delta\Sigma(12)}{\delta G(45)}\\&\quad\times G(46)\,G(75)\,\Lambda(673).\end{aligned} \tag{A5.18}$$

Keeping only the first term is the GW approximation of the background box below.9

Derivation: from the equation of motion to $\Sigma=\ii\hbar G\Lambda W$

A functional derivative obeys the rules of ordinary derivatives (product rule, chain rule) with integrals in place of sums over variables. The chain rule reads $\delta A(1)/\delta B(2)=\int\dd3\,[\delta A(1)/\delta C(3)]\,[\delta C(3)/\delta B(2)]$.

  1. The Heisenberg equation of the field operator, with the probe, is

    $$\begin{aligned}&\ii\hbar\,\partial_{t}\hat\psi(\br,t)=\Big[-\frac{\hbar^2\nabla^2}{2m_{\mathrm e}}+V^{\mathrm{ext}}(\br,t)\\&\;+\int\dd^3r'\,v(\br-\br')\,\hat n(\br',t)\Big]\\&\;\times\hat\psi(\br,t).\end{aligned}$$
    $\ii\hbar\,\partial_t\hat\psi=[\hat\psi,\hat H]$. With the anticommutation relations, the kinetic term gives the Laplacian and the Coulomb terms give the potential of all charges, electrons and nuclei in one density $\hat n$, because electron–electron and electron–nucleus interactions are the same $v$.

  2. Apply $\ii\hbar\partial_{t_1}$ to :

    $$\begin{aligned}&\Big[\ii\hbar\partial_{t_1}+\frac{\hbar^2\nabla_1^2}{2m_{\mathrm e}}-V^{\mathrm{ext}}(1)\Big]G(12)\\&=\delta(12)-\frac{\ii}{\hbar}\int\dd3\,v(1^+3)\\&\quad\times\langle\mathcal T\hat n(3)\hat\psi(1)\hat\psi^\dagger(2)\rangle .\end{aligned}$$
    The time derivative of the step functions in $\mathcal T$ gives the equal-time anticommutator, $\delta(\br_1-\br_2)\,\delta(t_1-t_2)$. The rest is step 1 inside the expectation value; the time $1^+$ keeps $\hat n$ to the left of $\hat\psi$.

  3. Schwinger's identity turns the three-operator average into a derivative: $\delta\langle\mathcal T\hat\psi(1)\hat\psi^\dagger(2)\rangle/\delta V^{\mathrm{ext}}(3)=-(\ii/\hbar)\,\langle\mathcal T[\hat n(3)-\langle\hat n(3)\rangle]\hat\psi(1)\hat\psi^\dagger(2)\rangle$. Hence $-(\ii/\hbar)\langle\mathcal T\hat n(3)\hat\psi(1)\hat\psi^\dagger(2)\rangle=\langle\hat n(3)\rangle G(12)+\ii\hbar\,\delta G(12)/\delta V^{\mathrm{ext}}(3)$.

    The identity of the main text with $\hat A=\hat\psi(1)$ and $\hat B=\hat\psi^\dagger(2)$. Multiplying it by $-\ii/\hbar$ and using the definition of $G$ separates the mean value $\langle\hat n(3)\rangle G(12)$ from the derivative.

  4. Insert step 3 into step 2. The mean value $\langle\hat n\rangle$ combines with $V^{\mathrm{ext}}$ into $V^{\mathrm{tot}}$ of :

    $$\begin{aligned}&\Big[\ii\hbar\partial_{t_1}+\frac{\hbar^2\nabla_1^2}{2m_{\mathrm e}}-V^{\mathrm{tot}}(1)\Big]G(12)\\&\quad-\ii\hbar\int\dd3\,v(1^+3)\,\frac{\delta G(12)}{\delta V^{\mathrm{ext}}(3)}=\delta(12).\end{aligned}$$
    The mean-field part is the Hartree potential of electrons and nuclei. Everything beyond the mean field is now in one functional derivative.

  5. Differentiating $\int\dd4\,G(14)G^{-1}(42)=\delta(12)$ gives $\delta G/\delta V^{\mathrm{ext}}=-G\,(\delta G^{-1}/\delta V^{\mathrm{ext}})\,G$, and the chain rule through $V^{\mathrm{tot}}$ with and gives $\delta G^{-1}(45)/\delta V^{\mathrm{ext}}(3)=-\int\dd6\,\Lambda(456)\,\varepsilon^{-1}(63)$. The last term of step 4 becomes

    $$\begin{aligned}&-\ii\hbar\int\dd(456)\,G(14)\,\Lambda(456)\\&\quad\times\Big[\int\dd3\,\varepsilon^{-1}(63)\,v(31^+)\Big]G(52)\\&=-\int\dd5\,\Sigma(15)\,G(52).\end{aligned}$$
    The bracket is $W(61^+)$ by . Renaming $4\to3$, $6\to4$, $5\to2$ in $\Sigma(15)=\ii\hbar\int\dd(46)\,G(14)\Lambda(456)W(61^+)$ gives , and the equation of motion becomes $[\dots-V^{\mathrm{tot}}]G-\Sigma G=\delta$, whose solution is the Dyson equation with $G^0$ defined by $[\dots-V^{\mathrm{tot}}]G^0=\delta$.

  6. The vertex equation : from step 5, $G^{-1}=(G^0)^{-1}-\Sigma$, and $(G^0)^{-1}$ depends on $V^{\mathrm{tot}}$ only through $-V^{\mathrm{tot}}(1)\,\delta(12)$. So $\Lambda(123)=\delta(12)\delta(13)+\delta\Sigma(12)/\delta V^{\mathrm{tot}}(3)$, and the chain rule through $G$, with $\delta G(45)/\delta V^{\mathrm{tot}}(3)=\int\dd(67)\,G(46)\Lambda(673)G(75)$, gives .

    $\Sigma$ depends on the potential only through $G$, as shows once $W$ and $\Lambda$ are expressed through $G$.

Screening: the Dyson equation for $W$

The screened interaction obeys a Dyson equation of its own, in four steps:

  1. Differentiate with respect to $V^{\mathrm{ext}}$: $\varepsilon^{-1}(12)=\delta(12)$ $+\int\dd3\,v(13)\,\delta\langle\hat n(3)\rangle/\delta V^{\mathrm{ext}}(2)$.

    The probe changes the total potential directly and through the charge it induces.

  2. The charges respond to the total potential they feel, so by the chain rule $\delta\langle\hat n(3)\rangle/\delta V^{\mathrm{ext}}(2)=\int\dd4\,\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}(34)\,\varepsilon^{-1}(42)$, with $\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}(34)=\delta\langle\hat n(3)\rangle/\delta V^{\mathrm{tot}}(4)$.

    $\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}$ is the response to the total potential, which already contains the field of the induced charge.

  3. Multiply step 1 by $v$ from the right and use : $W=v+v\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}W$.

    $\varepsilon^{-1}v=W$, and the second term of step 1 times $v$ becomes $v\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}\varepsilon^{-1}v=v\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}W$.

  4. Step 1 with step 2 reads $\varepsilon^{-1}=1+v\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}\varepsilon^{-1}$, so $\varepsilon=1-v\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}$.

    Multiply by $\varepsilon$ from the right; $1$ stands for $\delta(12)$.
$$\begin{gathered}W=v+v\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}W,\\ \chi^{\mathrm{irr}}(12)=\frac{\delta\langle\hat n(1)\rangle}{\delta V^{\mathrm{tot}}(2)},\\ \varepsilon=1-v\chi^{\mathrm{irr}},\qquad \varepsilon^{-1}=1+v\chi .\end{gathered} \tag{A5.19}$$
$\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}$
the irreducible polarizability of all charges: the induced density per unit change of the total potential (Å⁻⁶ eV⁻¹ in real space). It is negative for static perturbations: a more repulsive potential pushes charge away. With the nuclei clamped only the electrons contribute, and $W$ is the screened interaction of GW
$\chi$
the full, or reducible, density response, $\chi(12)=\delta\langle\hat n(1)\rangle/\delta V^{\mathrm{ext}}(2)$. Step 1 reads $\varepsilon^{-1}=1+v\chi$, and step 2 reads $\chi=\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}\varepsilon^{-1}$; together they give $\chi=\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}+\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}v\chi$
$\varepsilon$
the test-charge dielectric function: it screens the potential of a test charge that has no exchange or correlation with the medium

"Irreducible" means that $\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}$ contains no piece in which the induced charge acts back on the medium through its own bare Coulomb field: those pieces form the chain $\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}v\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}v\cdots$ that the Dyson equation sums. In a homogeneous medium every kernel depends only on $\br_1-\br_2$ and $t_1-t_2$, so the integrals in are convolutions, which a Fourier transform turns into products. Then $W=v+v\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}W$ gives $W(\bq,\omega)=v(q)/\varepsilon(\bq,\omega)$ with $\varepsilon=1-v(q)\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}(\bq,\omega)$, the relation used in the three models. Section A.3 used a test-electron dielectric function, which adds exchange and correlation between the screening electrons and an electron that feels the potential; the exact theory puts that extra screening into the vertex $\Lambda$ at the electron's end.10

Hedin's equations, the RPA and GW skip if familiar

For electrons in the field of clamped nuclei, Hedin (1965) wrote the exact many-electron problem as five coupled relations: $G$ from $\Sigma$ by the Dyson equation ; $\Sigma=\ii\hbar\,G\Lambda W$; the polarizability $\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}=-2\ii\hbar\,GG\Lambda$; $W=v+v\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}W$; and the vertex $\Lambda=1+(\delta\Sigma/\delta G)\,GG\Lambda$. Each quantity is built from the next one around a loop, often drawn as a pentagon.

Start the loop from $\Sigma=0$. The vertex is then $\Lambda(123)=\delta(12)\delta(13)$; the polarizability is $\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}(12)=-2\ii\hbar\,G(12)G(21^+)$, two propagators drawn as a closed loop (the "bubble"), which with Kohn–Sham propagators is the independent-particle response $\chi^0$ of Section A.3, the random-phase approximation (RPA); $W$ is the RPA screened interaction; and $\Sigma(12)=\ii\hbar\,G(12)W(21^+)$ is the GW approximation, named after its two factors. GW codes compute quasiparticle band structures in this way, and the Bethe–Salpeter equation for excitons uses the same $W$. Corrections to $\Lambda$ beyond the first term add exchange and correlation to the screening and to the self-energy.

The electrons alone: Hedin's equations

The density splits into an electronic and a nuclear part, and so does its response to the total potential. The electronic part follows from $G$, because the electron density is the propagator at equal times, with a factor 2 for the sum over spin. Differentiating with :

$$\begin{aligned}&\langle\hat n^{\rme}(1)\rangle=-2\ii\hbar\,G(11^+),\\&\chi^{\mathrm{irr,e}}(12)=\frac{\delta\langle\hat n^{\rme}(1)\rangle}{\delta V^{\mathrm{tot}}(2)}\\&\;=-2\ii\hbar\int\dd(34)\,G(13)\,G(41^+)\\&\;\times\Lambda(342),\\&W^{\rme}=v+v\chi^{\mathrm{irr,e}}W^{\rme},\\&\varepsilon^{\rme}=1-v\chi^{\mathrm{irr,e}} .\end{aligned} \tag{A5.20}$$
$\chi^{\mathrm{irr,e}}$
the electronic part of $\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}$
$W^{\rme}$, $\varepsilon^{\rme}$
the interaction screened by the electrons alone, and the corresponding test-charge dielectric function

The second form of $\chi^{\mathrm{irr,e}}$ uses $\delta G(11^+)/\delta V^{\mathrm{tot}}(2)$ $=\int\dd(34)\,G(13)\Lambda(342)G(41^+)$, which is $\delta G=-G\,\delta G^{-1}G$ combined with . If the nuclei are clamped at their sites, only the electrons respond, $\chi^{\mathrm{irr}}=\chi^{\mathrm{irr,e}}$ and $W=W^{\rme}$, and , , and are Hedin's equations (1965) for electrons in the field of fixed nuclei. In the GW approximation with Kohn–Sham propagators, $\chi^{\mathrm{irr,e}}$ becomes the $\chi^0$ of Section A.3, $\varepsilon^{\rme}$ its RPA dielectric function , and $W^{\rme}$ the screened interaction of a GW or Bethe–Salpeter calculation. In a crystal with a gap, at long wavelength and at frequencies far below the gap, $W^{\rme}\simeq v/\varepsilon_\infty$, the value used for the polar insulator.11

Letting the nuclei move: $W=W^{\rme}+W^{\ph}$

When the nuclei move, the field of an electron also pushes them. The displaced nuclei carry charge, the electrons screen that charge again, and its field acts on other electrons. The result is an extra, slow channel in the screened interaction: $W^{\rme}$ to a nucleus, propagation of the nuclear charge fluctuation, and $W^{\rme}$ again from the nucleus to the other electron. draws the result before the derivation, which follows the review and needs five steps.

  1. Write $W=\varepsilon^{-1}v=v+v\,\big[\delta\langle\hat n\rangle/\delta V^{\mathrm{ext}}\big]\,v$ and split $\hat n=\hat n^{\rme}+\hat n^{\ion}$. The electrons respond to the total potential, $\delta\langle\hat n^{\rme}\rangle/\delta V^{\mathrm{ext}}=\chi^{\mathrm{irr,e}}\varepsilon^{-1}$, so $W=v+v\chi^{\mathrm{irr,e}}W+v\,[\delta\langle\hat n^{\ion}\rangle/\delta V^{\mathrm{ext}}]\,v$. Move the second term to the left and multiply from the left by $(\varepsilon^{\rme})^{-1}=(1-v\chi^{\mathrm{irr,e}})^{-1}$:

    $$\begin{aligned}&W(12)=W^{\rme}(12)\\&\;+\int\dd(34)\,W^{\rme}(13)\\&\;\times\frac{\delta\langle\hat n^{\ion}(3)\rangle}{\delta V^{\mathrm{ext}}(4)}\,v(42).\end{aligned} \tag{A5.21}$$
    The first form of $W$ is step 1 of the screening derivation. $(\varepsilon^{\rme})^{-1}v=W^{\rme}$ by . The electrons now appear only through $W^{\rme}$, and the nuclei only through their response to the probe.

  2. Introduce a second probe, $V^{\mathrm{ext,ion}}$, that acts on the nuclei only, through $\int\dd^3r\,\hat n^{\ion}(\br)\,V^{\mathrm{ext,ion}}(\br,t)$. Then $\delta\langle\hat n^{\ion}(3)\rangle/\delta V^{\mathrm{ext}}(4)=\delta\langle\hat n(4)\rangle/\delta V^{\mathrm{ext,ion}}(3)$.

    By Schwinger's identity both sides equal $-(\ii/\hbar)\langle\mathcal T\,\delta\hat n^{\ion}(3)\,\delta\hat n(4)\rangle$, where $\delta\hat n=\hat n-\langle\hat n\rangle$: a probe inserts the density it couples to. In words, pushing on all charges and watching the nuclei is the same as pushing on the nuclei and watching all charges. This is a reciprocity relation.

  3. When the nuclear charge changes by $\delta\langle\hat n^{\ion}\rangle$, the electrons screen it, and the total potential changes by

    $$\int\dd4\,v(24)\,\delta\langle\hat n(4)\rangle=\int\dd5\,W^{\rme}(25)\,\delta\langle\hat n^{\ion}(5)\rangle .$$
    The electrons respond to the total potential: $\delta\langle\hat n^{\rme}\rangle=\chi^{\mathrm{irr,e}}v\,\delta\langle\hat n\rangle$, so $\delta\langle\hat n\rangle=(1-\chi^{\mathrm{irr,e}}v)^{-1}\delta\langle\hat n^{\ion}\rangle$ and $v\,\delta\langle\hat n\rangle=(1-v\chi^{\mathrm{irr,e}})^{-1}v\,\delta\langle\hat n^{\ion}\rangle=W^{\rme}\delta\langle\hat n^{\ion}\rangle$. The middle step holds because $v(1-\chi v)^{-1}$ and $(1-v\chi)^{-1}v$ are the same series, $v+v\chi v+v\chi v\chi v+\cdots$. The potential of a nuclear charge together with its electronic screening cloud is $W^{\rme}$ acting on that charge.

  4. The response of the nuclear charge to the nuclear probe is the nuclear density correlation function,

    $$\begin{aligned}&\chi^{\ion}(12)=\frac{\delta\langle\hat n^{\ion}(1)\rangle}{\delta V^{\mathrm{ext,ion}}(2)}\\&=-\tfrac{\ii}{\hbar}\langle\mathcal T\delta\hat n^{\ion}(1)\delta\hat n^{\ion}(2)\rangle\end{aligned} \tag{A5.22}$$
    Schwinger's identity once more. $\chi^{\ion}$ describes how a fluctuation of the nuclear charge created at 2 is found at 1. Inside it the nuclei interact with each other through the electrons that follow them; it is not a response of bare ions. It is symmetric, $\chi^{\ion}(12)=\chi^{\ion}(21)$, because the time ordering of two density operators does not depend on the order in which they are written.

  5. Assemble. By step 2, the integral over 4 in contains $\int\dd4\,v(24)\,\delta\langle\hat n(4)\rangle/\delta V^{\mathrm{ext,ion}}(3)$; by step 3 this is $\int\dd5\,W^{\rme}(25)\,\chi^{\ion}(53)$. Rename the points and use the symmetry of $\chi^{\ion}$.

    $v(42)=v(24)$, and step 3 holds for any change of the nuclear charge, in particular for the one caused by $V^{\mathrm{ext,ion}}$.

The result is the main formula of this section:12

$$\begin{aligned}W(12)&=W^{\rme}(12)+W^{\ph}(12),\\ W^{\ph}(12)&=\int\dd(34)\,W^{\rme}(13)\\&\qquad\times\chi^{\ion}(34)\,W^{\rme}(24).\end{aligned} \tag{A5.23}$$

Read from right to left, is the process of : an electron at 2 creates a potential screened by the electrons, $W^{\rme}(24)$, which pushes the nuclei at 4; the nuclear charge fluctuation propagates to 3, $\chi^{\ion}(34)$; and its field, screened again, acts on an electron at 1, $W^{\rme}(13)$. No approximation has been made so far: is exact for electrons and nuclei with Coulomb interactions. Hedin and Lundqvist first derived it in 1969.

Phonons inside $W$

The nuclear charge in terms of phonons

So far the nuclei are charge densities. Phonons appear when the delta functions of are expanded in the displacements. To second order, a Taylor expansion in $\bu$, with $\partial_\alpha$$\,=\partial/\partial r_\alpha$ as in Section A.2, gives

$$\begin{aligned}\delta(\br-\btau-\bu)={}&\delta(\br-\btau)-u_\alpha\partial_\alpha\delta(\br-\btau)\\&+\tfrac12u_\alpha u_\beta\,\partial_\alpha\partial_\beta\delta(\br-\btau),\end{aligned}$$

with repeated Cartesian indices summed. A delta function has no Taylor series of its own, but this one holds wherever the delta function stands inside an integral with a smooth function, such as the Coulomb potential that the nuclear charge creates. So

$$\begin{aligned}&\hat n^{\ion}(\br)=n^{\ion}_0(\br)\\&\;+\sum_{\ell\kappa}Z_\kappa\,\hat u_{\ell\kappa\alpha}\,\partial_\alpha\delta(\br-\btau_{\ell\kappa})\\&\;-\frac12\sum_{\ell\kappa}Z_\kappa\,\hat u_{\ell\kappa\alpha}\hat u_{\ell\kappa\beta}\\&\;\times\partial_\alpha\partial_\beta\delta(\br-\btau_{\ell\kappa}).\end{aligned} \tag{A5.24}$$
$n^{\ion}_0(\br)$
$-\sum_{\ell\kappa}Z_\kappa\,\delta(\br-\btau_{\ell\kappa})$, the static lattice of point charges

Each term has a picture. The first is the crystal at rest. The second is a lattice of point dipoles, $Z_\kappa\hat\bu_{\ell\kappa}$, one for each displaced nucleus: the seed of the polar coupling of Section A.4. The third smears each nucleus over the region it explores by its vibrations, which will give the Debye–Waller correction of Section A.7. Truncating at second order is the harmonic approximation of this theory, the counterpart of the truncation of the energy surface $U$ in Section A.1. A fluctuation of the nuclear charge is, to first order in the displacements, the dipole term. Inserting the displacement operator of Section A.1, , writes it as a sum over phonons:

$$\begin{aligned}&\delta\hat n^{\ion}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_\ell}}\sum_{\bq\nu}\Delta_{\bq\nu}n^{\ion}\,\hat\phi_{\bq\nu},\\&\Delta_{\bq\nu}n^{\ion}=\sum_{\ell\kappa\alpha}\Big(\frac{\hbar}{2M_\kappa\omega_{\bq\nu}}\Big)^{1/2}Z_\kappa\\&\;\times e_{\kappa\alpha,\nu}(\bq)\,\ee^{\ii\bq\cdot\bR_\ell}\\&\;\times\partial_\alpha\delta(\br-\btau_{\ell\kappa}).\end{aligned} \tag{A5.25}$$
$\delta\hat n^{\ion}$
the fluctuation $\hat n^{\ion}-\langle\hat n^{\ion}\rangle$ at $(\br,t)$, here its dipole part; the phonon field is taken at the same time $t$
$\Delta_{\bq\nu}n^{\ion}(\br)$
the change of the nuclear charge density per unit phonon field $\hat\phi_{\bq\nu}$: the $\Delta_{\bq\nu}$ operation of Section A.2 applied to $\hat n^{\ion}$ (Å⁻³)

The factors are those of : the zero-point amplitude, the eigenvector $e_{\kappa\alpha,\nu}(\bq)$, the phase of the cell, and $1/\sqrt{N_\ell}$ with $N_\ell$ the number of cells. Keeping only this linear term inside $\chi^{\ion}$ is the one-phonon approximation: the dropped terms, products of three or four displacements, describe processes with two phonons at once.13

The phonon propagator

The density fluctuation is a sum of phonon fields, so its correlation function is built from the correlation function of the phonon fields. That object is the phonon propagator:

$$\begin{aligned}&F_{\nu\nu'}(\bq,t)\\&\;=-\frac{\ii}{\hbar}\langle\mathcal T\,\hat\phi_{\bq\nu}(t)\,\hat\phi^\dagger_{\bq\nu'}(0)\rangle,\\&F^0_\nu(\bq,\omega)=\frac{2\omega_{\bq\nu}/\hbar}{\omega^2-\omega^2_{\bq\nu}+\ii\eta}\\&\;\text{or, retarded, }\frac{2\omega_{\bq\nu}/\hbar}{(\omega+\ii\eta)^2-\omega^2_{\bq\nu}}.\end{aligned} \tag{A5.26}$$
$F_{\nu\nu'}(\bq,\omega)$
phonon propagator: $\ii\hbar F$ is the amplitude for a lattice wave $\bq$ excited in branch $\nu'$ at time 0 to be found in branch $\nu$ at time $t$. It carries one wavevector because crystal momentum is conserved, and it has units of 1/energy (eV⁻¹) after the Fourier transform in time
$F^0_\nu(\bq,\omega)$
the same for free harmonic phonons of frequency $\omega_{\bq\nu}$, those of the force constants of Section A.1; it is diagonal in $\nu$

$F^0$ has poles at $\omega=\pm\omega_{\bq\nu}$, where a phonon of energy $\hbar\omega_{\bq\nu}$ is created or absorbed. Its numerator $2\omega_{\bq\nu}/\hbar$ comes from combining the two poles, one from each term of $\hat\phi_{\bq\nu}=\hat a_{\bq\nu}+\hat a^\dagger_{-\bq\nu}$. The retarded form is the causal response: it vanishes before the perturbation acts, which places $\omega+\ii\eta$ in the denominator. Later sections use it for physical responses, and it does not depend on temperature. A phonon propagator with interactions has shifted and broadened poles; Section A.6 computes them.14

Derivation: the free phonon propagator

  1. For free phonons, $\hat\phi_{\bq\nu}(t)=\hat a_{\bq\nu}\ee^{-\ii\omega_{\bq\nu}t}+\hat a^\dagger_{-\bq\nu}\ee^{\ii\omega_{\bq\nu}t}$, and $\hat\phi^\dagger_{\bq\nu}=\hat a^\dagger_{\bq\nu}+\hat a_{-\bq\nu}$.

    Each mode is an independent oscillator with the phonon Hamiltonian of Section A.1, so $\hat a_{\bq\nu}(t)=\hat a_{\bq\nu}\ee^{-\ii\omega_{\bq\nu}t}$; and $\omega_{-\bq\nu}=\omega_{\bq\nu}$.

  2. In the phonon vacuum only $\langle\hat a\hat a^\dagger\rangle=1$ survives. For $t>0$, $\langle\hat\phi_{\bq\nu}(t)\hat\phi^\dagger_{\bq\nu}(0)\rangle=\ee^{-\ii\omega_{\bq\nu}t}$; for $t<0$ the time ordering swaps the operators and $\langle\hat\phi^\dagger_{\bq\nu}(0)\hat\phi_{\bq\nu}(t)\rangle=\ee^{\ii\omega_{\bq\nu}t}$. So $F^0_\nu(\bq,t)=-(\ii/\hbar)\,\ee^{-\ii\omega_{\bq\nu}|t|}$.

    $\hat a|0\rangle=0$ removes every other product; for $t<0$ the surviving pair is $\hat a_{-\bq\nu}\hat a^\dagger_{-\bq\nu}$.

  3. Transform with $\ee^{\ii\omega t}$, adding $\ee^{-\eta|t|}$ for convergence: $F^0_\nu(\bq,\omega)=\hbar^{-1}\big[(\omega-\omega_{\bq\nu}+\ii\eta)^{-1}-(\omega+\omega_{\bq\nu}-\ii\eta)^{-1}\big]$, which is the time-ordered form of .

    $\int_0^\infty\dd t\,\ee^{\ii(\omega-\omega_{\bq\nu}+\ii\eta)t}=\ii/(\omega-\omega_{\bq\nu}+\ii\eta)$, and similarly for $t<0$.

  4. The retarded function, $-(\ii/\hbar)\theta(t)\langle[\hat\phi_{\bq\nu}(t),\hat\phi^\dagger_{\bq\nu}(0)]\rangle=-(2/\hbar)\,\theta(t)\sin\omega_{\bq\nu}t$, with $\theta$ the unit step function, transforms to the retarded form of .

    The commutator of two free phonon fields is a number, $-2\ii\sin\omega_{\bq\nu}t$, the same in every state: this is why the retarded $F^0$ does not depend on temperature.

Now insert the phonon fields into $\chi^{\ion}$ and $W^{\ph}$, in three steps:

  1. Insert into . Since $\delta\hat n^{\ion}$ is Hermitian, write it at point 2 with $\hat\phi^\dagger$ and complex-conjugated coefficients; crystal momentum is conserved, so only equal wavevectors survive:

    $$\begin{aligned}&\chi^{\ion}(12)=\tfrac1{N_\ell}\sum_{\bq\nu\nu'}\\&\;\Delta_{\bq\nu}n^{\ion}(\br_1)\\&\;\times F_{\nu\nu'}(\bq,t_1-t_2)\\&\;\times\Delta_{-\bq\nu'}n^{\ion}(\br_2)\end{aligned} \tag{A5.27}$$
    A lattice translation multiplies $\hat\phi_{\bq\nu}$ by a phase $\ee^{\ii\bq\cdot\bR_\ell}$ and leaves the ground state unchanged, so $\langle\hat\phi_{\bq\nu}\hat\phi^\dagger_{\bq'\nu'}\rangle$ vanishes unless $\bq'=\bq$. The conjugate coefficient is $[\Delta_{\bq\nu}n^{\ion}]^*=\Delta_{-\bq\nu}n^{\ion}$, by $e_{\kappa\alpha,\nu}(-\bq)=e^*_{\kappa\alpha,\nu}(\bq)$ and $\omega_{-\bq\nu}=\omega_{\bq\nu}$ (Section A.1).

  2. Insert into . Each $W^{\rme}$ acts on one factor $\Delta_{\bq\nu}n^{\ion}$, the bare vertex of the nuclei, and the combination is the potential of that charge change screened by the electrons:

    $$\begin{aligned}&\int\dd^3r'\,W^{\rme}(\br,\br';\omega)\,\Delta_{\bq\nu}n^{\ion}(\br')\\&=\int\dd^3r'\,(\varepsilon^{\rme})^{-1}(\br,\br';\omega)\\&\quad\times\Delta_{\bq\nu}V^{\mathrm{en}}(\br') .\end{aligned}$$
    $W^{\rme}=(\varepsilon^{\rme})^{-1}v$, and $v$ acting on $\Delta_{\bq\nu}n^{\ion}$ is the change of the electron–nucleus potential, $\Delta_{\bq\nu}V^{\mathrm{en}}=\int\dd^3r'\,v(\br-\br')\,\Delta_{\bq\nu}n^{\ion}(\br')$, by the definition of $\hat V^{\mathrm{en}}$ under .

  3. Fourier transform in time. The two time integrals in are convolutions, which become products at one frequency $\omega$.

    A chain $\int\dd t_3\,\dd t_4\,A(t_1-t_3)B(t_3-t_4)C(t_2-t_4)$ transforms to $A(\omega)B(\omega)C(-\omega)$. The time-ordered $W^{\rme}$ of a crystal with time-reversal symmetry is even in $\omega$, so $C(-\omega)=C(\omega)$.

The result is the lattice part of the screened interaction written with phonons:

$$\begin{aligned}&W^{\ph}(\br_1,\br_2;\omega)\\&\;=\frac1{N_\ell}\sum_{\bq\nu\nu'}\mathcal V_{\bq\nu}(\br_1,\omega)\,F_{\nu\nu'}(\bq,\omega)\\&\;\times\mathcal V_{-\bq\nu'}(\br_2,\omega),\\&\mathcal V_{\bq\nu}(\br,\omega)\\&\;=\int\dd^3r'\,(\varepsilon^{\rme})^{-1}(\br,\br';\omega)\\&\;\times\Delta_{\bq\nu}V^{\mathrm{en}}(\br').\end{aligned} \tag{A5.28}$$
$\mathcal V_{\bq\nu}(\br,\omega)$
the screened vertex of the phonon $\bq\nu$: the bare potential change per unit phonon field, screened by the electrons at frequency $\omega$ (eV)

$W^{\ph}$ is a phonon exchanged between two screened vertices. At $\br_1$ an electron absorbs a phonon $\bq\nu$ (or emits $-\bq\nu$), the phonon propagates, and at $\br_2$ an electron absorbs $-\bq\nu'$: crystal momentum $\hbar\bq$ flows from the electron at $\br_2$ to the electron at $\br_1$. When the screening is static, $(\varepsilon^{\rme})^{-1}$ is real and $\mathcal V_{-\bq\nu}=\mathcal V^*_{\bq\nu}$, so the second vertex is the complex conjugate of the first. The factor $1/N_\ell$ is the square of the $N_\ell^{-1/2}$ that each vertex carries in the Hamiltonian of Section A.2, . For the Einstein oscillators of , each ion is its own mode, and reduces to : the vertex is the zero-point amplitude times the force, up to sign.15

The vertex: a screened gradient of the nuclear potential

$\Delta_{\bq\nu}V^{\mathrm{en}}$ is the potential change that a phonon would produce if the electrons did not respond: the rigid-ion potential change of Section A.2, a sum of gradients of the nuclear potentials weighted by the zero-point amplitudes. The vertex $\mathcal V_{\bq\nu}$ is this change screened by the electrons, with the exact many-body dielectric function. Its matrix element between Bloch states is the electron–phonon matrix element of Section A.2, , and DFPT computes it with a specific approximation:

$$\begin{aligned}&g_{mn\nu}(\bk,\bq)\\&\;=\langle\psi_{m\bk+\bq}|\Delta_{\bq\nu}V^{\mathrm{KS}}|\psi_{n\bk}\rangle\\&\;\simeq\langle\psi_{m\bk+\bq}|\mathcal V_{\bq\nu}(\br,0)|\psi_{n\bk}\rangle .\end{aligned} \tag{A5.29}$$

The self-consistent potential change of DFPT is $\Delta_{\bq\nu}V^{\mathrm{KS}}=(\varepsilon^{\rme})^{-1}\Delta_{\bq\nu}V^{\mathrm{en}}$, , with $V^{\mathrm{KS}}$ the Kohn–Sham potential. So the DFPT vertex is the many-body vertex $\mathcal V_{\bq\nu}(\br,\omega)$ with three approximations: the screening is static, $\omega=0$; it is computed in the RPA with a local exchange–correlation kernel, the test-electron form of Section A.3; and the Bloch states are Kohn–Sham states. This identification is the main link between Part A's first-principles practice and the exact theory.16

The frequency dependence of the screening, which this primer calls dynamical screening, is the lag of the electrons behind the ions met in Section A.2. The review calls it retardation, following Bardeen and Pines (1955) and Baym (1961). Hedin and Lundqvist replaced $(\varepsilon^{\rme})^{-1}(\omega)$ by its static value, which amounts to the Born–Oppenheimer approximation for the vertex. In insulators the difference is small, because the electronic excitations cost much more than a phonon. In metals the screening of a slow lattice wave is not static; Section A.6 shows the consequences for the phonons.17

Which "retardation"

Three ideas share the word. A retarded function is a causal response, with $\omega+\ii\eta$. The review's retardation effects are the frequency dependence of the electronic screening, the dynamical screening of this primer: the electrons need time to respond. The EPP manuscript's retardation is the finite speed of light. In this section the speed of light is infinite, because $v(12)$ is instantaneous; Section X.1 takes up the third idea.

Both ends of the phonon line in carry screened vertices, since an electron feels the phonon through the screened potential and the phonon is pushed by the screened field of the electron. This matters later. The phonon self-energy of Section A.6 turns out to contain one bare and one screened vertex, and using two screened vertices there would count the screening twice.

The polar insulator again: Fröhlich's coupling

The general result reproduces the polar insulator among the simple models above and explains its residue, in three steps:

  1. At long wavelength in a polar crystal, the vertex of the LO phonon, with static screening, is dominated by the macroscopic potential of its dipole wave, which is a plane wave: $\mathcal V_{\bq,\mathrm{LO}}(\br)\simeq g^{\mathrm{lr}}(\bq)\,\ee^{\ii\bq\cdot\br}$, with $g^{\mathrm{lr}}$ the long-range vertex of Section A.4 in its isotropic, one-mode form, Fröhlich's , whose modulus depends only on $q=|\bq|$.

    The dipole wave carries the polarization charge density $-\ii\bq\cdot\bP^{\ion}$, whose potential is $4\pi/q^2$ times that charge density: for a longitudinal wave it grows as $1/q$ and dominates every other part of the vertex as $q\to0$. The electrons screen it with $\varepsilon_\infty$.

  2. Insert into :

    $$\begin{aligned}&W^{\ph}(\br_1,\br_2;\omega)\\&\;=\frac1{N_\ell}\sum_\bq|g^{\mathrm{lr}}(q)|^2F^0_{\mathrm{LO}}(\omega)\,\ee^{\ii\bq\cdot(\br_1-\br_2)} .\end{aligned}$$
    Only the LO branch carries a macroscopic field, so only $\nu=\nu'=\mathrm{LO}$ contributes. The second vertex is $\mathcal V_{-\bq,\mathrm{LO}}=\mathcal V^*_{\bq,\mathrm{LO}}$ (static screening), so $g^{\mathrm{lr}}(-\bq)=g^{\mathrm{lr}}(\bq)^*$. With static screening the phonon propagator is the free one, $F^0$ (shown after below), and at long wavelength its LO pole is at $\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}$.

  3. Read off the Fourier component per unit volume: $W^{\ph}(\bq,\omega)=\OV\,|g^{\mathrm{lr}}(q)|^2\,F^0_{\mathrm{LO}}(\omega)$.

    A function of $\br_1-\br_2$ is $(1/\OVSC)\sum_\bq W(\bq)\,\ee^{\ii\bq\cdot(\br_1-\br_2)}$, the convention in which $v(q)=4\pi e^2/q^2$, where $\OVSC$$\,=N_\ell\OV$ is the volume of the Born–von Kármán supercell of Section A.1; so the factor $1/N_\ell$ becomes $\OV/\OVSC$.

Inserting $F^0_{\mathrm{LO}}$ from and Fröhlich's matrix element gives

$$\begin{aligned}&W^{\ph}(\bq,\omega)=\OV\,|g^{\mathrm{lr}}(q)|^2\\&\;\times\frac{2\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}/\hbar}{\omega^2-\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}^2},\\&|g^{\mathrm{lr}}(q)|^2=\frac{2\pi e^2\hbar\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}}{\OV\,q^2}\\&\;\times\Big(\frac1{\varepsilon_\infty}-\frac1{\varepsilon_{\mathrm s}}\Big).\end{aligned} \tag{A5.30}$$

The product is $v(q)(1/\varepsilon_\infty-1/\varepsilon_{\mathrm s})\,\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}^2/(\omega^2-\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}^2)$, exactly the $W^{\ph}$ of . So the residue of $W$ at the LO pole in $\omega$ is $\OV|g^{\mathrm{lr}}(q)|^2/\hbar$, Fröhlich's coupling squared up to the factor $\OV/\hbar$, and the classical dielectric function and the many-body theory agree. In GaAs, $|g^{\mathrm{lr}}(q)|\,q=32$ meV Å⁻¹, so $|g^{\mathrm{lr}}|=0.32$ eV at $q=0.1$ Å⁻¹, a tenth of the way from $\Gamma$ to the zone boundary; the coupling grows without bound as $q\to0$. The polar vertex, the dielectric constants and the LO–TO splitting are three faces of one object, the lattice part of $W$.18

Phonons are nuclei interacting through $W^{\rme}$

The phonon propagator needs an equation of its own. Its content is Newton's law for the nuclei: mass times acceleration equals the Coulomb force of all other charges. That force has to be expressed through the quantities of the theory. Take two different nuclei, $\ell\kappa$ and $\ell'\kappa'$, and move the second one:

  1. Displacing nucleus $\ell'\kappa'$ by $\bu_{\ell'\kappa'}(t')$ adds a point dipole to the nuclear charge, $\delta n^{\ion}(\br,t')=Z_{\kappa'}u_{\ell'\kappa'\beta}(t')\,\partial_\beta\delta(\br-\btau_{\ell'\kappa'})$.

    This is the linear term of .

  2. Its potential, screened by the electrons, is

    $$\begin{aligned}&\delta V^{\mathrm{tot}}(\br,t)=-Z_{\kappa'}\int\dd t'\\&\;\times\partial'_\beta W^{\rme}(\br,\btau_{\ell'\kappa'};t-t')\,u_{\ell'\kappa'\beta}(t'),\end{aligned}$$

    where $\partial'_\beta$ acts on the second argument.

    By step 3 of the derivation of , the potential of a nuclear charge with its screening cloud is $W^{\rme}$ acting on that charge; an integration by parts moves the derivative from the delta function to $W^{\rme}$. The cloud forms over time, so the potential at $t$ depends on the displacement at earlier times $t'$.

  3. Nucleus $\ell\kappa$, of charge $-Z_\kappa$ in units of $-e$, has the energy $-Z_\kappa\,\delta V^{\mathrm{tot}}(\btau_{\ell\kappa},t)$, so the force on it is $F_{\ell\kappa\alpha}=Z_\kappa\,\partial_\alpha\delta V^{\mathrm{tot}}(\btau_{\ell\kappa},t)$.

    A force is minus the gradient of the energy with respect to the position of the particle.

  4. Compare with the force constants of Section A.1, whose force law is $F_{\ell\kappa\alpha}$$\,=-\sum$$\Phi$$\,u$. At frequency $\omega$ the convolution in time becomes a product, and the force constant between the two nuclei is $Z_\kappa Z_{\kappa'}\,\partial_\alpha\partial'_\beta W^{\rme}(\btau_{\ell\kappa},\btau_{\ell'\kappa'};\omega)$.

    Steps 2 and 3 give $F_{\ell\kappa\alpha}=-Z_\kappa Z_{\kappa'}\int\dd t'\,\partial_\alpha\partial'_\beta W^{\rme}(t-t')\,u_{\ell'\kappa'\beta}(t')$.

  5. The block of a nucleus with itself follows from the sum rule. When the whole crystal is moved slowly, $\omega\to0$, no force may arise, so each row of the static force constants sums to zero, as in . This fixes the static part of the on-site block as minus the sum of the static couplings to all other nuclei.

    The on-site block also contains the force that a nucleus feels from its own screening cloud when the cloud lags behind the nucleus; that part depends on frequency. Baym obtained the complete expression from the equation of motion of the displacements, with an external force on the nuclei as the probe; the sum rule fixes the part that comes from the static charge distribution.

The result, due to Baym (1961), is a force-constant matrix that depends on frequency:19

$$\begin{aligned}&\Phi_{\ell\kappa\alpha,\ell'\kappa'\beta}(\omega)\\&=Z_\kappa Z_{\kappa'}\,\partial_\alpha\partial'_\beta W^{\rme}(\btau_{\ell\kappa},\btau_{\ell'\kappa'};\omega)\\&\quad-\delta_{\ell\ell'}\delta_{\kappa\kappa'}\sum_{\ell''\kappa''}Z_\kappa Z_{\kappa''}\\&\qquad\times\partial_\alpha\partial'_\beta W^{\rme}(\btau_{\ell\kappa},\btau_{\ell''\kappa''};0).\end{aligned} \tag{A5.31}$$
$\Phi_{\ell\kappa\alpha,\ell'\kappa'\beta}(\omega)$
dynamical force constants: minus the force along $\alpha$ on nucleus $\ell\kappa$ per unit displacement of nucleus $\ell'\kappa'$ along $\beta$, for a displacement that oscillates at frequency $\omega$ (eV/Å²)
$\partial_\alpha$, $\partial'_\beta$
derivatives with respect to the first and the second argument of $W^{\rme}$, taken at the equilibrium positions

In words: the phonons are vibrations of point nuclei that interact through $W^{\rme}$, the Coulomb interaction screened by the electrons. On the diagonal, both terms contain the bare $v$ of a nucleus with itself, which is infinite; because $v$ does not depend on frequency, it cancels in their difference, $Z_\kappa^2\,\partial\partial'[W^{\rme}(\omega)-W^{\rme}(0)]$ at coincident points. At $\omega=0$ the second term enforces the many-body acoustic sum rule,

$$\sum_{\ell'\kappa'}\Phi_{\ell\kappa\alpha,\ell'\kappa'\beta}(0)=0 , \tag{A5.32}$$

which is the acoustic sum rule of Section A.1. Baym derived it for a crystal held in place by fictitious restoring forces that keep each nucleus near its site, so that the crystal as a whole cannot drift or rotate. At $\omega=0$, is the force-constant matrix $\Phi$ of Section A.1: the second derivative of the Born–Oppenheimer energy, with the static screening of the electrons treated exactly. DFPT computes it with the RPA-plus-exchange–correlation screening of Section A.3. The frequency dependence of $\Phi(\omega)$ is the nonadiabatic correction: the part that the adiabatic approximation of Section A.2 leaves out, because there the electrons follow the nuclei instantly, as in the Born–Oppenheimer approximation. It is tiny in insulators and important in metals (Section A.6).20

Jellium checks the result. For point ions of charge $Ze$, one per cell, the lattice Fourier transform of is a sum over the wavevectors $\bq+\bG$. In the jellium limit, where the ions form a uniform background, only the term $\bG=0$ survives, and its longitudinal component is $(Z^2/\OV)\,q^2\,W^{\rme}(q,\omega)$. Newton's equation, with $W^{\rme}$ taken at $\omega=0$, sets $M\omega^2$ equal to this component, and with $W^{\rme}=4\pi e^2/[q^2\varepsilon^{\rme}(q)]$ this gives $\omega^2=4\pi Z^2e^2/[M\OV\varepsilon^{\rme}(q)]=(\omega_{\mathrm p}^{\ion})^2/\varepsilon^{\rme}(q)$: exactly the pole $\omega_{\mathrm{LA}}(q)$ of $W$ in . The phonon frequency follows either from Baym's equation for the nuclei or from the pole of Hedin's screened interaction, and the two agree.

In the phonon basis, the equation of motion fixes the inverse of the phonon propagator:

$$\begin{aligned}&F^{-1}_{\nu\nu'}(\bq,\omega)\\&\;=\frac{\hbar\,\big[\omega^2\delta_{\nu\nu'}-\tPhi_{\nu\nu'}(\bq,\omega)\big]}{2\sqrt{\omega_{\bq\nu}\omega_{\bq\nu'}}},\\&\tPhi_{\nu\nu'}(\bq,\omega)=\sum_{\kappa\alpha,\kappa'\beta}e^*_{\kappa\alpha,\nu}(\bq)\\&\;\times\tPhi_{\kappa\alpha,\kappa'\beta}(\bq,\omega)\,e_{\kappa'\beta,\nu'}(\bq).\end{aligned} \tag{A5.33}$$
$\tPhi_{\kappa\alpha,\kappa'\beta}(\bq,\omega)$
the dynamical matrix of $\Phi(\omega)$: its lattice Fourier transform divided by $\sqrt{M_\kappa M_{\kappa'}}$, as in
$\tPhi_{\nu\nu'}(\bq,\omega)$
the same matrix in the basis of the phonon eigenvectors (eV Å⁻² amu⁻¹, like $\omega^2$)

With static screening, $\Phi(\omega)\to\Phi(0)$, the eigenvectors diagonalize the dynamical matrix, $\tPhi_{\nu\nu'}(\bq,0)=\omega^2_{\bq\nu}\delta_{\nu\nu'}$ (the eigenvalue equation and orthonormality of Section A.1), and becomes $1/F^0_\nu$: the free phonons of are the Born–Oppenheimer phonons. The poles of $F$ are the solutions of $\det\big[\omega^2-\tPhi(\bq,\omega)\big]=0$, the eigenvalue problem of Section A.1 with a dynamical matrix that depends on the frequency it is solved for. Section A.6 writes this as a Dyson equation, $F=F^0+F^0\,$$\Pi^{\ph}$$\,F$, whose phonon self-energy is the frequency-dependent part of $\Phi(\omega)$ in the phonon basis: by , $\Pi^{\ph}_{\nu\nu'}(\bq,\omega)$ $=\hbar\big[\tPhi_{\nu\nu'}(\bq,\omega)-\tPhi_{\nu\nu'}(\bq,0)\big]/2\sqrt{\omega_{\bq\nu}\omega_{\bq\nu'}}$.21

Derivation: the phonon propagator from the dynamical force constants

  1. Baym's equation of motion for the displacement propagator $\mathcal U_{\ell\kappa\alpha,\ell'\kappa'\beta}(\omega)$, the Fourier transform of $-(\ii/\hbar)\langle\mathcal T\hat u_{\ell\kappa\alpha}(t)\hat u_{\ell'\kappa'\beta}(0)\rangle$, is $\sum\big[M_\kappa\omega^2\delta-\Phi(\omega)\big]\,\mathcal U(\omega)=1$, a matrix equation over the labels $\ell\kappa\alpha$.

    It is Newton's equation of Section A.1 with the force constants , in the frequency domain. For one free oscillator it gives $\mathcal U=1/[M(\omega^2-\omega_0^2)]$, the driven-oscillator response of .

  2. By , $\hat u_{\ell\kappa\alpha}=\sum_{\bq\nu}S_{\ell\kappa\alpha,\bq\nu}\hat\phi_{\bq\nu}$ with $S_{\ell\kappa\alpha,\bq\nu}=(\hbar/2N_\ell M_\kappa\omega_{\bq\nu})^{1/2}e_{\kappa\alpha,\nu}(\bq)\,\ee^{\ii\bq\cdot\bR_\ell}$, so $\mathcal U=S\,F\,S^\dagger$ and $F^{-1}=S^\dagger\big[M\omega^2-\Phi(\omega)\big]S$.

    $\hat u$ is Hermitian, so the second displacement can be written as $\hat u^\dagger=\sum S^*\hat\phi^\dagger$; $S$ is square and invertible.

  3. $S^\dagger MS=\hbar/2\omega_{\bq\nu}$ on the diagonal, and $S^\dagger\Phi(\omega)S$ is diagonal in $\bq$ and equals $\hbar\,\tPhi_{\nu\nu'}(\bq,\omega)/2\sqrt{\omega_{\bq\nu}\omega_{\bq\nu'}}$. Together these give .

    The lattice sum $\sum_\ell\ee^{\ii(\bq'-\bq)\cdot\bR_\ell}=N_\ell\delta_{\bq\bq'}$ and translation invariance turn $\Phi$ into its Fourier transform, as in the derivation of ; the orthonormality of the eigenvectors does the rest.

The quadratic term of survives in the mean nuclear density. Since $\langle\hat\bu_{\ell\kappa}\rangle=0$ (the equilibrium positions are the mean positions of the nuclei),

$$\begin{aligned}&\langle\hat n^{\ion}(\br)\rangle=n^{\ion}_0(\br)\\&\;-\frac12\sum_{\ell\kappa}Z_\kappa\,\langle\hat u_{\ell\kappa\alpha}\hat u_{\ell\kappa\beta}\rangle\\&\;\times\partial_\alpha\partial_\beta\delta(\br-\btau_{\ell\kappa}),\end{aligned} \tag{A5.34}$$

with the mean-square displacements of Section A.1, or more generally the phonon propagator at equal times. To second order this is each point charge spread into a cloud whose width is the amplitude of its zero-point and thermal motion. The smeared charge enters $V^{\mathrm{tot}}$ and gives the Debye–Waller self-energy of Section A.7.22

The Hedin–Baym equations

The equations of this section now close on themselves. Written symbolically, with products standing for integrals over internal points, they are

$$\begin{aligned}\langle\hat n^{\rme}\rangle&=-2\ii\hbar\,G(11^+),\\ \langle\hat n^{\ion}\rangle&=n^{\ion}_0-\tfrac12Z\langle\hat u\hat u\rangle\partial\partial\delta,\\ V^{\mathrm{tot}}&=v\,\big(\langle\hat n^{\rme}\rangle+\langle\hat n^{\ion}\rangle\big),\\ G&=G^0+G^0\Sigma G,\\ \Sigma&=\ii\hbar\,G\Lambda\,\big(W^{\rme}+W^{\ph}\big),\\ \Lambda&=1+\frac{\delta\Sigma}{\delta G}\,GG\Lambda,\\ \chi^{\mathrm{irr,e}}&=-2\ii\hbar\,GG\Lambda,\\ W^{\rme}&=v+v\,\chi^{\mathrm{irr,e}}W^{\rme},\\ W^{\ph}&=\tfrac1{N_\ell}\sum\mathcal V F\mathcal V,\\ \mathcal V&=(\varepsilon^{\rme})^{-1}\Delta V^{\mathrm{en}},\\ F^{-1}&\propto\omega^2-\tPhi(\omega),\\ \Phi(\omega)&=ZZ'\partial\partial'W^{\rme}(\omega)\\&\quad-(\text{static self term}).\end{aligned} \tag{A5.35}$$

Line by line: the densities of electrons and nuclei ; the total potential with the probe switched off; the Dyson equation for the electrons ; the self-energy with $W=W^{\rme}+W^{\ph}$ ; the vertex ; the electronic polarizability and the electron-screened interaction ; the phonon part of the screened interaction ; and the equation of motion of the phonons, with . The electronic equations are Hedin's (1965), the nuclear ones Baym's (1961), and the review collects them as the Hedin–Baym equations. shows how they feed each other.23

Three properties make the set the reference for everything that follows.

  • It is not perturbative. The equations fix the exact propagators self-consistently; nothing is expanded in powers of a coupling constant.
  • It does not assume Born–Oppenheimer. $\Phi(\omega)$ and the vertex keep their frequency dependence, so the same equations cover insulators, doped semiconductors and metals.
  • It contains Hedin's equations. Setting $F=0$ removes $W^{\ph}$ and the smearing of the nuclei, and what remains is Hedin's equations for clamped nuclei, the framework of GW. With the nuclei free, electrons and nuclei meet in only three places: through $\varepsilon^{\rme}$ and $W^{\rme}$, which build the vertex $\mathcal V$ of $W^{\ph}$ and the force constants $\Phi(\omega)$; through $W^{\ph}$ in $\Sigma$; and through $\langle\hat n^{\ion}\rangle$ in $V^{\mathrm{tot}}$. The set contains no separate coupling constant: the coupling is the electronic screening of the nuclear charge. This is why the review calls the electronic dielectric function "absolutely central".

What the Hedin–Baym equations leave out

The set is harmonic: it keeps the expansion to second order, and it keeps the one-phonon term inside $\chi^{\ion}$. Going beyond the harmonic approximation is possible in principle but leads to a formalism of forbidding complexity (Gillis, 1970). The set is written at zero temperature; finite temperatures need the Matsubara formalism, which works with propagators in imaginary time, and Sections A.7 and A.8 use its results. The interaction is the instantaneous Coulomb interaction, so there are no transverse photons and the speed of light is infinite. Finally, nobody solves the set as it stands: Sections A.6–A.8 introduce the approximations of practice, namely the GW vertex, static screening and DFPT phonons.

How the review writes these objects

The review works in SI units with spin labels, writes the probes as $\varphi$, $J$ and $\mathbf F_{\kappa p}$, the polarizations as $P$ and $P_{\rm e}$, the vertex as $\Gamma$, and the screened interactions as $W_{\rm e}$ and $W_{\rm ph}$. One letter, $D$, serves for the nuclear density correlation function $D(12)$ (our $\chi^{\ion}$), the displacement correlation function $D_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}$ and the mode propagator $D_{\mathbf q\nu\nu'}$ (our $\hbar F$); only the arguments tell them apart. Its phonon self-energy $\Pi_{\kappa\alpha p,\kappa'\alpha'p'}(\omega)$ has the units of force constants and is our $\Phi(\omega)$.

Where these objects go next

Section A.6 solves the phonon equation as a Dyson equation and splits the self-energy into the adiabatic part, which DFPT computes, and the nonadiabatic rest, with one bare and one screened vertex. Section A.7 inserts $W^{\ph}$ of into the self-energy , which gives the Fan–Migdal self-energy, and adds the Debye–Waller term from the smeared nuclei . Section A.8 turns both into band gaps that change with temperature, and Section A.9 uses the frequency-dependent attraction of jellium in the theory of superconductivity.

Every bare line in is the instantaneous Coulomb interaction , coupled to charge densities. The EPP formalism of Part B keeps it as the longitudinal part of the photon propagator, adds the transverse photons, and couples both to currents (Sections X.1 and B.4). Section B.9 shows that the electron-screened interaction $W^{\rme}$ is one sector of the photon propagator dressed by the electrons, $D^{\rme}_{\rho\rho}$. It also recovers $W=W^{\rme}+W^{\ph}$ when the speed of light goes to infinity, with RPA screening and with the long-range (dipole) part of the vertex only: the ions of the EPP Lagrangian couple to the field through their Born-charge dipoles.24

Check yourself: three short questions

  1. In a polar insulator, what are $W(\bq,0)$ and $W(\bq,\omega)$ for $\omega\gg\omega_{\mathrm{LO}}$ (but below the gap), in terms of $v(q)$? Why do they differ?

    Answer. $v/\varepsilon_{\mathrm s}$ and $v/\varepsilon_\infty$, from and . A static charge is screened by both clouds; far above the phonon frequencies the ions cannot follow, and only the electrons screen. In GaAs the ratio is $\varepsilon_\infty/\varepsilon_{\mathrm s}=0.85$.

  2. Clamp the nuclei in the Hedin–Baym equations . Which lines change, and what remains?

    Answer. With $F=0$, $W^{\ph}=0$ and $\langle\hat n^{\ion}\rangle=n^{\ion}_0$, a rigid lattice of point charges; the phonon equation is no longer needed. What remains are Hedin's equations for electrons in the field of fixed nuclei: in the GW approximation, the GW method.

  3. Bare ions of sodium oscillate at $\hbar\omega_{\mathrm p}^{\ion}=29.6$ meV for every wavevector. Why are the phonons of jellium acoustic, and what is their sound velocity?

    Answer. The electrons screen the ions, $\omega_{\mathrm{LA}}^2=(\omega_{\mathrm p}^{\ion})^2/\varepsilon^{\rme}(q)$ by , and Thomas–Fermi screening gives $\varepsilon^{\rme}\simeq k_{\mathrm{TF}}^2/q^2$ at small $q$. So $\omega_{\mathrm{LA}}\simeq(\omega_{\mathrm p}^{\ion}/k_{\mathrm{TF}})\,q$, with $v_{\mathrm s}=(29.6\ \text{meV}/\hbar)/(1.49\ \text{Å}^{-1})=4.50\times10^{13}\ \text{s}^{-1}\times0.671\ \text{Å}=3.0$ km/s.
